identity.title: Spectral Perturbation Bounds for Low-Rank Approximation with Applications to Privacy

problem.claim: Understand how noise and measurement errors affect low-rank approximations in spectral norm, especially for differentially private approximation.

gap.claim: Prior analyses often use Frobenius error or reconstruction quality, which may misrepresent subspace distortion.

contributions.claim: New high-probability spectral-norm perturbation bounds for symmetric matrices that model interactions between A and arbitrary symmetric E.
A contour bootstrapping approach from complex analysis, extended to spectral functionals including polynomials and matrix exponentials.
Improved utility guarantees for differentially private PCA, reported as resolving an open literature problem.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that their perturbation bounds refine Eckart–Young–Mirsky and that their contour bootstrapping method is novel and broadly extended.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report sharp estimates for ||(A+E)_p−A_p|| under mild eigengap and norm conditions, with improvements of up to a factor of √n.
The authors report improved differentially private PCA utility guarantees and describe them as resolving an open problem.
On real-world datasets, the authors report that the bounds closely track actual spectral error across diverse perturbation regimes.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames spectral-norm sensitivity of low-rank approximation as a central challenge and highlights differential privacy.
It contrasts spectral norm with commonly used Frobenius or reconstruction metrics, arguing the latter can misestimate subspace distortion.
It introduces high-probability perturbation bounds for symmetric matrices and states improvements under eigengap and norm conditions.
It presents contour bootstrapping extensions and applies the analysis to differentially private PCA.
It reports close agreement between bounds and observed spectral error on real-world datasets.

source_observation.claim: The abstract ties the chosen error metric to the target notion of subspace distortion and utility, then states explicit improvement and applicability conditions.

lessons.interpretation: A paper can make its technical contribution more assessable by aligning the evaluation metric with the failure mode and preserving the conditions attached to guarantees.
lessons.application: When presenting a perturbation result, define the operational error metric, state the assumptions beside the bound, and quantify improvement against the relevant baseline.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the application objective is reconstruction fidelity rather than worst-case directional or subspace error.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact eigengap and norm conditions, probability level, or bound formulas.
The reported factor-√n improvement lacks a named baseline and regime details.
Dataset identities, perturbation constructions, and quantitative empirical errors are not given.
The open problem claimed to be resolved is not identified.
